question.es: ¿Qué significaba «nice» en inglés antes de significar «simpático»?
question.en: What did the English word “nice” used to mean before it meant “pleasant”?

answer.es: Significaba «tonto» o «ignorante»: viene del latín «nescius», el que no sabe.
answer.en: It meant “foolish” or “ignorant” — from Latin “nescius”, one who does not know.

detail.es: En el siglo XIII «nice» describía a alguien necio o descuidado. Antes de instalarse en «agradable» en el siglo XVIII pasó por «lascivo», «extravagante» y «quisquilloso»: pocos adjetivos ingleses han cambiado tanto de sentido.
detail.en: In the 1200s “nice” described someone careless or clueless. Before settling on “pleasant” in the 1700s it drifted through “lascivious,” “extravagant” and “fussy” — few English adjectives have flipped meaning so many times.

_evidence: "foolish, ignorant, frivolous, senseless," from Old French nice (12c.) "careless, clumsy;

question.es: ¿Qué quería decir «awful» en inglés antes de significar «horrible»?
question.en: What did “awful” mean in English before it meant “terrible”?

answer.es: Lo contrario: significaba «leno de asombro reverente», de «awe-ful».
answer.en: The opposite: it meant “full of reverent awe,” from “awe-ful.”

detail.es: Hacia 1300 describía algo que imponía respeto o temor sagrado, como una catedral o un rey. La versión rebajada de «muy malo» no aparece hasta 1809, y la de «muchísimo» como simple intensificador hasta 1818.
detail.en: Around 1300 it described something that struck people with reverence or sacred dread, like a cathedral or a king. The watered-down sense of “very bad” only shows up by 1809, and “extremely” as a plain intensifier by 1818.

_evidence: c. 1300, agheful, aueful, "worthy of respect or fear, striking with awe; causing dread" ... The weakened sense of "very bad" is by 1809; the weakened sense of "excessively; very great" is by 1818.

question.es: ¿Qué significaba «silly» en inglés antiguo antes de significar «tonto»?
question.en: What did “silly” mean in Old English before it meant “foolish”?

answer.es: «Bendito» y «feliz»: viene del inglés antiguo «gesælig».
answer.en: “Blessed” and “happy” — it comes from Old English “gesælig.”

detail.es: Pasó de «feliz» a «bendito», luego a «inocente» y «digno de lástima», y solo hacia 1570 aterrizó en «tonto». Comparte raíz con el alemán «selig», que hoy sigue significando «bienaventurado».
detail.en: It drifted from “happy” to “blessed,” then to “innocent” and “pitiable,” only landing on “foolish” around 1570. It shares a root with German “selig,” which still means “blessed” today.

_evidence: Middle English seli, seely, from Old English gesælig "happy, fortuitous, prosperous" ... The word's considerable sense development moved it by various streams from "happy" through "blessed;" "pious;" "innocent" ... to "feeble in mind, lacking in reason, foolish" (1570s).

question.es: ¿A quién nombraba «girl» en el inglés medieval, solo a las niñas?
question.en: Did “girl” in medieval English only refer to female children?

answer.es: No: en el siglo XIII nombraba a cualquier criatura joven, niño o niña.
answer.en: No — in the 1300s it meant any young person, boy or girl alike.

detail.es: «Gyrle» empezó siendo «niño, persona joven» sin distinción de sexo. El significado se estrechó a «niña» a finales del siglo XIV, y no hay consenso sobre de dónde salió la palabra antes de eso.
detail.en: “Gyrle” started out meaning “child, young person” regardless of sex. The narrower sense of “female child” only took hold in the late 1300s, and where the word came from before that is still unresolved.

_evidence: c. 1300, gyrle "child, young person" (of either sex but most frequently of females)

question.es: ¿Por qué en inglés medieval una zanahoria podía llamarse «meat»?
question.en: Why could a medieval English cook call a carrot “meat”?

answer.es: Porque «meat» significaba «comida» en general, no solo carne.
answer.en: Because “meat” simply meant “food” in general, not flesh specifically.

detail.es: Viene del inglés antiguo «mete», sustento o nutrición; las verduras se llamaban «grene-mete» y los lácteos «white meat». El sentido estrecho de «carne animal» no se impuso hasta alrededor del año 1300.
detail.en: It comes from Old English “mete,” meaning nourishment or sustenance; vegetables were called “grene-mete” and dairy “white meat.” The narrow sense of “animal flesh” only took over around 1300.

_evidence: Middle English mēte, from Old English mete "food, nourishment, sustenance"

question.es: ¿Por qué «sinister» en inglés viene de la palabra latina para «izquierda»?
question.en: Why does English “sinister” come from the Latin word for “left”?

answer.es: Porque los augures romanos leían los presagios a la izquierda como de mal agüero.
answer.en: Because Roman augurs read omens seen on the left as bad luck.

detail.es: Los vuelos de aves observados a mano izquierda se interpretaban como señal de desgracia, así que «sinister» («izquierdo» en latín) pasó a significar «desfavorable». De ahí saltó a «malintencionado» en el siglo XV.
detail.en: Bird flights observed on the left hand were read as a sign of misfortune, so “sinister” (Latin for “left”) came to mean “unfavorable.” From there it jumped to “ill-intentioned” by the 1400s.

_evidence: sinister "left, on the left side" (opposite of dexter) ... The Latin word was used in augury in the sense of "unlucky, unfavorable" (omens, especially bird flights, seen on the left hand were regarded as portending misfortune)

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver un «companion» en inglés con compartir el pan?
question.en: What does an English “companion” have to do with sharing bread?

answer.es: Todo: la palabra viene del latín «cum panis», literalmente «con quien comparte pan».
answer.en: Everything: the word comes from Latin “cum panis,” literally “the one you share bread with.”

detail.es: El latín tardío «companio» designaba al compañero de mesa, al que se sentaba a comer contigo. La misma lógica aparece en el gótico «gahlaiba», «compañero de pan», así que la idea no es solo romana.
detail.en: Late Latin “companio” named the one who ate at your table. The same logic shows up in Gothic “gahlaiba,” “bread-fellow,” so the idea wasn’t only Roman.

_evidence: from Late Latin companionem (nominative companio), etymologically "bread fellow, messmate," from Latin com "with, together" + panis "bread"

question.es: ¿Por qué a los aspirantes a un cargo se les llama «candidatos»?
question.en: Why are people running for office called “candidates”?

answer.es: Porque en Roma se presentaban con una toga blanqueada a mano: la «toga candida».
answer.en: Because in Rome they showed up in a hand-whitened toga: the “toga candida.”

detail.es: La blanqueaban con tiza fina para insinuar pureza de intenciones. «Candidatus» significaba literalmente «vestido de blanco», de la misma raíz que «candela» o «incandescente».
detail.en: It was whitened with fine chalk to suggest purity of intent. “Candidatus” literally meant “clothed in white,” from the same root as “candle” or “incandescent.”

_evidence: White was the usual color of the Roman toga, but office-seekers in ancient Rome wore a gleaming white toga (toga candida), probably whitened with fine powdered chalk, presumably to indicate the purity of their intentions in seeking a role in civic affairs.

question.es: ¿Qué tienen que ver «glamour» y «gramática»?
question.en: What do “glamour” and “grammar” have in common?

answer.es: Son la misma palabra: «glamour» nació como una deformación escocesa de «grammar».
answer.en: They’re the same word: “glamour” started as a Scottish twist on “grammar.”

detail.es: En la Edad Media «grammar» significaba también «saber erudito», y por extensión «saber oculto»: quien leía y escribía parecía manejar magia. De ahí que «gramarye» pasara a significar «hechizo» antes de suavizarse en «encanto».
detail.en: In medieval times “grammar” also meant “scholarly learning” and, by extension, “occult knowledge”: anyone who could read and write looked like they wielded magic. That’s how “gramarye” came to mean “spell” before softening into “charm.”

_evidence: a variant of Scottish gramarye "magic, enchantment, spell," said to be an alteration of English grammar in a specialized use of that word's medieval sense of "any sort of scholarship, especially occult learning"

question.es: ¿Por qué «bancarrota» lleva la palabra «banco» dentro?
question.en: Why does the word for “bankruptcy” carry “bank” inside it?

answer.es: Porque viene del italiano «banca rotta»: el banco, el mueble, roto.
answer.en: Because it comes from Italian “banca rotta”: a broken bench.

detail.es: Los prestamistas italianos trabajaban desde un banco o mesa en la calle. Se contaba que si se arruinaban, ese mueble se rompía en público; etymonline avisa de que la costumbre probablemente era más figurada que literal, pero la imagen dio nombre a la palabra.
detail.en: Italian moneylenders worked from a bench or table set up in the street. The story goes that when one went under, the bench was broken in public; etymonline notes the custom was probably more figurative than literal, but the image gave the word its name.

_evidence: from Italian banca rotta, literally "a broken bench," from banca "moneylender's shop," literally "bench" ... it is said to have been called so from an old custom of breaking the bench of bankrupts, [but] the allusion probably is figurative

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver el toque de queda con apagar el fuego?
question.en: What does a curfew have to do with putting out a fire?

answer.es: Todo: «curfew» viene del francés «cuevrefeu», literalmente «cubrir fuego».
answer.en: Everything: “curfew” comes from French “cuevrefeu,” literally “cover fire.”

detail.es: En la Edad Media una campana avisaba a los vecinos, con casas de madera y paja pegadas unas a otras, de que era hora de tapar las brasas del hogar para no incendiar el pueblo entero. La orden de recogerse llegó después.
detail.en: In medieval times a bell told villagers, whose wood-and-straw houses stood close together, to smother their hearth embers so the whole town wouldn’t catch fire. The order to stay indoors came later.

_evidence: from Anglo-French coeverfu (late 13c.), from Old French cuevrefeu, literally "cover fire" (Modern French couvre-feu), from cuevre, imperative of covrir "to cover" ... + feu "fire"

question.es: ¿Qué significaba «naughty» en inglés antes de significar «travieso»?
question.en: What did “naughty” mean in English before it meant “mischievous”?

answer.es: «Pobre», literalmente «que no tiene nada»: viene de «naught», cero.
answer.en: “Poor,” literally “having nothing” — it comes from “naught,” zero.

detail.es: En el siglo XIV describía a alguien indigente, sin bienes. Pasó por «malvado» y «inmoral» antes de suavizarse, hacia 1630, en la travesura infantil que conserva hoy.
detail.en: In the 1300s it described someone destitute, with nothing to their name. It passed through “wicked” and “immoral” before softening, by the 1630s, into the childish mischief it means today.

_evidence: late 14c., nowghty, noughti "needy, having nothing," also "evil, immoral, corrupt, unclean," from nought, naught

question.es: ¿Qué era un «villano» antes de ser el malo de la película?
question.en: What was a “villain” before becoming the bad guy of the story?

answer.es: Un campesino: alguien que trabajaba la tierra de un señor feudal.
answer.en: A peasant: someone who worked the land for a feudal lord.

detail.es: Viene del latín «villanus», «habitante de la villa o finca». La nobleza urbana empezó a usarlo con desprecio hacia el siglo XVI, y de ahí saltó a «capaz de maldad»; el personaje de ficción no aparece hasta 1822.
detail.en: It comes from Latin “villanus,” “inhabitant of the villa, or farm.” Urban nobility started using it contemptuously by the 1500s, and from there it jumped to “capable of wickedness”; the fictional character sense only shows up in 1822.

_evidence: from Medieval Latin villanus "farmhand," from Latin villa "country house, farm"

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver «fornicar» con la arquitectura romana?
question.en: What does the word “fornicate” have to do with Roman architecture?

answer.es: Viene de «fornix», el arco: en Roma, las prostitutas se ofrecían bajo los arcos.
answer.en: It comes from “fornix,” arch: in Rome, prostitutes solicited from under the arches.

detail.es: «Fornix» significaba «bóveda, arco, pasaje cubierto», y por extensión «burdel», porque las prostitutas romanas trabajaban bajo esas estructuras. El sustantivo pasó al inglés hacia 1300; el verbo tardó otros 250 años en aparecer.
detail.en: “Fornix” meant “vault, arch, covered passage,” and by extension “brothel,” because Roman prostitutes worked under those structures. The noun entered English around 1300; the verb took another 250 years to show up.

_evidence: from Latin fornix (genitive fornicis) "brothel" ... originally "arch, vaulted chamber, a vaulted opening, a covered way" ... The sense extension in Latin is perhaps because Roman prostitutes commonly solicited from under the arches of certain buildings.

question.es: ¿Qué llevaba puesto un guerrero «berserk» para merecer ese nombre?
question.en: What was a “berserk” warrior wearing to earn that name?

answer.es: Probablemente una piel de oso: «berserkr» es «camisa de oso» en nórdico antiguo.
answer.en: Probably a bearskin: “berserkr” is “bear shirt” in Old Norse.

detail.es: Los guerreros nórdicos que combatían en un estado de furia ritual daban nombre al adjetivo inglés moderno. Una teoría del siglo XIII, del escritor Snorri Sturluson, decía que significaba «sin camisa»; los etimólogos actuales la descartan a favor de «piel de oso».
detail.en: Norse warriors who fought in a trance-like fury gave the modern English adjective its name. A 13th-century theory by the writer Snorri Sturluson claimed it meant “shirtless”; today’s etymologists reject that in favor of “bearskin.”

_evidence: probably from ber- "bear" + serkr "shirt," thus literally "a warrior clothed in bearskin" ... not, as Scott evidently believed, from Old Norse berr "bare, naked" and meaning "warrior who fights without armor."

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver una «nightmare» con un caballo?
question.en: What does a “nightmare” have to do with a horse?

answer.es: Nada: ese «mare» es un demonio nocturno, no una yegua.
answer.en: Nothing: that “mare” is a night demon, not a female horse.

detail.es: En inglés antiguo «mare» nombraba a un íncubo que se sentaba sobre el pecho del durmiente y le cortaba la respiración, provocando sueños angustiosos. Solo hacia mediados del siglo XVI el significado se trasladó del demonio a la sensación de ahogo que causaba.
detail.en: In Old English “mare” named an incubus that sat on a sleeper’s chest and cut off their breath, causing anguished dreams. Only by the mid-1500s did the meaning shift from the demon itself to the suffocating feeling it caused.

_evidence: "night-goblin, incubus, oppressed sleep," Old English mare "incubus, nightmare, monster; witch, sorcerer"

question.es: ¿De verdad los romanos juraban agarrándose los testículos, y de ahí viene «testificar»?
question.en: Did Romans really swear oaths by grabbing their testicles, giving us the word “testify”?

answer.es: No: es un mito medieval. «Testis» viene de una raíz que significa «tercero», el testigo neutral.
answer.en: No — that’s a medieval myth. “Testis” comes from a root meaning “third party,” the neutral witness.

detail.es: Existen muchos relatos de juramentos romanos y ninguno menciona los testículos; la leyenda es una invención posterior. Es verdad que los romanos también usaban «testis» como eufemismo para testículo, por la idea de que era «testigo» de la virilidad, y esa coincidencia alimentó el mito.
detail.en: There are plenty of accounts of Roman oaths and none mention testicles; the legend is a later invention. Romans did also use “testis” as a euphemism for testicle, on the idea that it “witnessed” virility, and that coincidence is what fed the myth.

source: World Wide Words — Swearing on Testicles
_evidence: The Latin word for a witness was testis, which derives from an Indo-European word for the number three... There really is a strong link between testicle and testify... but those who swear by this belief have misunderstood the matter.

question.es: ¿Por qué en inglés al caimán lo llaman «alligator»?
question.en: Why do English speakers call the caiman an “alligator”?

answer.es: Porque los colonos ingleses deformaron el español «el lagarto».
answer.en: Because English colonists mangled the Spanish phrase “el lagarto.”

detail.es: Los exploradores españoles en Florida llamaban al animal «el lagarto (de Indias)». Los ingleses se quedaron con la frase entera, artículo incluido, y la convirtieron en una sola palabra con una «r» que nunca estuvo ahí, como en «tater» o «feller».
detail.en: Spanish explorers in Florida called the animal “el lagarto (de Indias),” the lizard. English speakers kept the whole phrase, article and all, and folded it into one word with an extra “r” that was never really there, the way “tater” or “feller” picked one up.

_evidence: a corruption of Spanish el lagarto (de Indias) "the lizard (of the Indies)," from Latin lacertus

question.es: ¿Por qué en inglés se dice «an orange» y no «a norange»?
question.en: Why do English speakers say “an orange” and not “a norange”?

answer.es: Porque la «n» inicial se confundió con el artículo y se perdió por el camino.
answer.en: Because the initial “n” got mistaken for the article and dropped along the way.

detail.es: La palabra viene del sánscrito «naranga», pasó al persa, al árabe y al italiano antiguo «narancia». En frases como «una narancia» sonaba como si la «n» perteneciera al artículo, así que varias lenguas la soltaron: quedó «arancia», «orange», «an orange».
detail.en: The word comes from Sanskrit “naranga,” passing through Persian, Arabic and Old Italian “narancia.” In phrases like “una narancia” the “n” sounded like it belonged to the article, so several languages dropped it: it became “arancia,” “orange,” “an orange.”

_evidence: from Sanskrit naranga-s "orange tree," a word of uncertain origin ... Loss of initial n- probably is due to confusion with the definite article (as in une narange, una narancia)

question.es: ¿Qué significaba la palabra que dio origen a «azúcar» antes de referirse al dulce?
question.en: What did the word behind “sugar” originally mean before it referred to anything sweet?

answer.es: «Gravilla» o «arenilla»: es lo que significa el sánscrito «sharkara».
answer.en: “Grit” or “gravel” — that’s what the Sanskrit “sharkara” originally meant.

detail.es: El azúcar cristalizada recordaba a granos de arena, así que el nombre se quedó. La palabra viajó del sánscrito al persa «shakar», al árabe «sukkar» y al latín medieval antes de llegar al español y al inglés casi sin cambios.
detail.en: Crystallized sugar looked like grains of sand, so the name stuck. The word traveled from Sanskrit to Persian “shakar,” to Arabic “sukkar,” to Medieval Latin before reaching Spanish and English almost unchanged.

_evidence: from Sanskrit sharkara "ground or candied sugar," originally "grit, gravel"

question.es: ¿Por qué unos países dicen «té» y otros «chai» si es la misma planta?
question.en: Why do some countries say “tea” and others “chai” for the same plant?

answer.es: Porque es la misma palabra china repartida por dos rutas comerciales distintas.
answer.en: Because it’s the same Chinese word, spread by two different trade routes.

detail.es: Quien lo compró por mar a comerciantes de Fujian, como los holandeses, se quedó con «te»; quien lo recibió por tierra, por la Ruta de la Seda, desde el mandarín «cha», dice «chai» o parecido. Español, inglés y ruso dividen el mundo entre esos dos sonidos.
detail.en: Whoever bought it by sea from Fujian traders, like the Dutch, kept “te”; whoever received it overland via the Silk Road, from Mandarin “cha,” says “chai” or something close. Spanish, English and Russian split the world between those two sounds.

_evidence: Russian chai, Persian cha, Greek tsai, Arabic shay, and Turkish çay all came by overland trade routes from the Mandarin form.

question.es: ¿Por qué a un magnate de los negocios se le llama «tycoon»?
question.en: Why is a business magnate called a “tycoon”?

answer.es: Porque era el título con que los extranjeros llamaban al sogún de Japón.
answer.en: Because it was the title foreigners used for the shogun of Japan.

detail.es: «Taikun», «gran señor», llegó al inglés tras la visita del comodoro Perry a Japón en 1853. Los secretarios de Abraham Lincoln lo adoptaron como apodo cariñoso para el presidente; de ahí saltó a «persona poderosa» en general, y ya en el siglo XX a «empresario rico».
detail.en: “Taikun,” “great lord,” entered English after Commodore Perry’s 1853 visit to Japan. Lincoln’s secretaries adopted it as an affectionate nickname for the president; from there it jumped to “powerful person” in general, and by the 20th century to “wealthy businessman.”

_evidence: 1857, title given by foreigners to the shogun of Japan, from Japanese taikun "great lord or prince" ... the transferred meaning of "important person" is attested by 1861 [in ref. to Lincoln, in the diary of his secretary, John Hay]

question.es: ¿Por qué a un contorno recortado en negro se le llama «silueta»?
question.en: Why is a black cutout outline called a “silhouette”?

answer.es: Por burla: llevaba el nombre de un ministro francés famoso por recortar gastos.
answer.en: As a mockery: it carries the name of a French minister famous for cutting costs.

detail.es: Étienne de Silhouette fue ministro de Finanzas en 1759 y propuso recortes impopulares entre la nobleza. Todo lo que parecía barato o escueto empezó a llamarse «a la Silhouette», y el apodo se quedó pegado justo a los retratos más baratos que había: las sombras recortadas.
detail.en: Étienne de Silhouette was finance minister in 1759 and proposed cuts unpopular with the nobility. Anything that looked cheap or bare-bones started being called “à la Silhouette,” and the nickname stuck to the cheapest portraits around: cut-out shadow profiles.

_evidence: The usual reason given (by 1766 in French sources) is that it was a derisive reference to Silhouette's petty economies, unpopular among the nobility, to finance France during the Seven Years' War.

question.es: ¿Quién era «Boycott», el hombre que le dio nombre al boicot?
question.en: Who was “Boycott,” the man who gave his name to the boycott?

answer.es: Un administrador de fincas en Irlanda al que sus vecinos dejaron de hablar en 1880.
answer.en: An estate agent in Ireland whom his neighbors stopped speaking to in 1880.

detail.es: El capitán Charles Boycott exigía rentas abusivas a los arrendatarios de lord Erne. Siguiendo un llamamiento político a aislar sin violencia a los caseros abusivos, sus trabajadores, mozos de cuadra y servicio doméstico lo abandonaron en bloque. La prensa bautizó la táctica con su apellido en cuestión de semanas.
detail.en: Captain Charles Boycott was demanding extortionate rents from Lord Erne’s tenants. Following a political call to isolate abusive landlords without violence, his laborers, stable hands and household staff walked out on him en masse. The press named the tactic after him within weeks.

_evidence: Captain Charles Cunningham Boycott (12 March 1832 – 19 June 1897) was an English land agent whose ostracism by his local community in Ireland gave the English language the term boycott.

question.es: ¿Por qué la sustancia adictiva del tabaco se llama «nicotina»?
question.en: Why is the addictive substance in tobacco called “nicotine”?

answer.es: Por el embajador francés que mandó las primeras semillas de tabaco a París.
answer.en: After the French ambassador who sent the first tobacco seeds to Paris.

detail.es: Jean Nicot era embajador de Francia en Portugal y en 1561 envió semillas y hojas de tabaco en polvo a la corte francesa, convencido de sus propiedades medicinales. Los botánicos bautizaron la planta «Nicotiana» en su honor, y de ahí salió el nombre del alcaloide.
detail.en: Jean Nicot was France’s ambassador to Portugal, and in 1561 he sent tobacco seeds and powdered leaves to the French court, convinced of its medicinal value. Botanists named the plant “Nicotiana” in his honor, and the alkaloid took its name from there.

_evidence: named for Jean Nicot (c. 1530-1600), French ambassador to Portugal, who sent tobacco seeds and powdered leaves from Lisbon to France 1561

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver una rebeca de lana con una carga de caballería suicida?
question.en: What does a wool cardigan have to do with a suicidal cavalry charge?

answer.es: Lleva el nombre del conde que dirigió esa carga: el conde de Cardigan.
answer.en: It’s named after the earl who led that charge: the Earl of Cardigan.

detail.es: James Brudenell, séptimo conde de Cardigan, dirigió en 1854 la desastrosa Carga de la Brigada Ligera contra la artillería rusa en Crimea. Volvió a Gran Bretaña convertido en celebridad y llevando el chaleco de punto que popularizó, y que terminó llevando su título.
detail.en: James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan, led the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade against Russian artillery in Crimea in 1854. He came home a celebrity, wearing the knitted waistcoat he made fashionable — and which ended up carrying his title.

_evidence: The person in this case was James Thomas Brudenell, seventh earl of Cardigan... In October 1854, at the age of 57, he led the disastrous charge of the Light Brigade up the valley towards the Russian guns... It would seem his name became attached to it because he was the best-known figure of the War, who was fêted on his return to Britain and lived extravagantly.

question.es: ¿Por qué el saxofón se llama exactamente así?
question.en: Why is the saxophone called exactly that?

answer.es: Por el apellido de quien lo inventó: el belga Adolphe Sax.
answer.en: After the surname of the man who invented it: the Belgian Adolphe Sax.

detail.es: Sax lo diseñó hacia 1840 combinando la boquilla de un clarinete con el cuerpo de metal de un fagot. Su apellido se pegó al invento junto con el sufijo griego «-fono», «que suena».
detail.en: Sax designed it around 1840, combining a clarinet mouthpiece with the brass body of a bassoon. His surname stuck to the invention along with the Greek suffix “-phone,” meaning “sounding.”

_evidence: named for Antoine Joseph "Adolphe" Sax (1814-1894), Belgian instrument maker who devised it c. 1840

question.es: ¿Existió de verdad el «magnetismo animal» que da nombre a «mesmerizar»?
question.en: Did the “animal magnetism” behind the word “mesmerize” actually exist?

answer.es: No como fluido físico: era la teoría de un médico austríaco, Franz Mesmer.
answer.en: Not as a physical fluid: it was the theory of an Austrian physician, Franz Mesmer.

detail.es: Mesmer sostenía en el siglo XVIII que un fluido invisible circulaba entre los cuerpos y que él podía manipularlo para curar. La teoría no resistió el escrutinio científico, pero la palabra sobrevivió: hoy «mesmerizar» es sinónimo de dejar a alguien hipnotizado.
detail.en: Mesmer claimed in the 1700s that an invisible fluid ran between bodies and that he could steer it to heal people. The theory didn’t survive scientific scrutiny, but the word did: today “mesmerize” just means leaving someone spellbound.

_evidence: named for Franz Anton Mesmer (1734-1815), Austrian physician who developed a theory of animal magnetism and a mysterious body fluid which allows one person to hypnotize another

question.es: ¿Existió de verdad el soldado que dio nombre al «chovinismo»?
question.en: Did the soldier behind the word “chauvinism” actually exist?

answer.es: Nadie lo sabe con certeza: pudo ser un personaje inventado para una obra de teatro.
answer.en: Nobody knows for sure — he may have been invented for a stage play.

detail.es: Nicolas Chauvin, veterano obsesionado con Napoleón mucho después de su caída, apareció en un vodevil francés de 1831 como caricatura del patriotismo ciego. Los etimólogos no han logrado identificar con certeza a una persona real detrás del personaje, pero el apellido ya se había fijado a la palabra.
detail.en: Nicolas Chauvin, a veteran obsessed with Napoleon long after his fall, showed up in an 1831 French vaudeville as a caricature of blind patriotism. Etymologists haven’t been able to pin down a real person behind the character, but the surname had already stuck to the word.

_evidence: from the character Nicholas Chauvin, soldier of Napoleon's Grand Armee, who idolized Napoleon and the Empire long after it was history ... if there was a real person at the base of the character in the play, he has not been certainly identified by etymologists

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver una salamandra con manipular un mapa electoral?
question.en: What does a salamander have to do with rigging an electoral map?

answer.es: La forma de un distrito trazado a mano se pareció a una, y el nombre se quedó.
answer.en: A hand-drawn district ended up shaped like one, and the name stuck.

detail.es: En 1812 el gobernador de Massachusetts, Elbridge Gerry, aprobó un mapa de distritos diseñado para favorecer a su partido. Uno de ellos, en el condado de Essex, tenía una forma tan retorcida que un periódico lo dibujó como una salamandra y fundió el apellido de Gerry con el animal.
detail.en: In 1812 Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry approved a district map designed to favor his party. One district, in Essex County, was so twisted in shape that a newspaper drew it as a salamander and fused Gerry’s surname with the animal.

_evidence: Gerry, governor of Massachusetts, was lampooned when his party redistricted the state in a blatant bid to preserve an Antifederalist majority. One sprawling Essex County district resembled a salamander, and a newspaper editor dubbed it the Gerrymander.

question.es: ¿Por qué a quien no sigue las reglas del grupo se le llama «maverick»?
question.en: Why is someone who won’t follow the group called a “maverick”?

answer.es: Por un ganadero tejano que nunca marcaba a hierro su ganado.
answer.en: After a Texas rancher who never branded his cattle.

detail.es: Samuel Maverick era tan descuidado con el hierro que sus reses sueltas y sin marcar se conocieron por su apellido en todo el sur de Texas. Cuando vendió el rebaño, el comprador reclamó como suyas todas las reses sin marca que encontró, y la palabra saltó de las vacas a las personas que no se dejan encasillar.
detail.en: Samuel Maverick was so careless with the branding iron that his loose, unmarked cattle became known by his name across South Texas. When he sold the herd, the buyer claimed every unbranded head he could round up as his own, and the word jumped from cattle to people who refuse to be pigeonholed.

_evidence: so called for Samuel A. Maverick (1803-1870), Texas cattle owner who was notoriously negligent in branding his calves.

question.es: ¿Qué medía la arroba (@) antes de servir para escribir un correo?
question.en: What did the @ symbol measure before it was used to write an email address?

answer.es: Ánforas de vino: la usaban los mercaderes para no escribir la palabra entera.
answer.en: Jars of wine: merchants used it so they wouldn’t have to write the whole word out.

detail.es: La primera vez documentada que aparece es en una carta de 1536 de un mercader florentino, Francesco Lapi, para abreviar «ánfora» al hablar de precios del vino en Sevilla. En español y portugués sobrevivió como unidad de peso, la arroba, antes de que el correo electrónico le diera un segundo trabajo.
detail.en: The earliest documented appearance is in a 1536 letter by Florentine merchant Francesco Lapi, abbreviating “amphora” while quoting wine prices in Seville. In Spanish and Portuguese it survived as a unit of weight, the “arroba,” long before email gave it a second job.

source: Smithsonian Magazine — The Accidental History of the @ Symbol
_evidence: The first documented use was in 1536, in a letter by Francesco Lapi, a Florentine merchant, who used @ to denote units of wine called amphorae, which were shipped in large clay jars.

question.es: ¿Por qué el símbolo «&» tiene un nombre tan raro en inglés, «ampersand»?
question.en: Why does the “&” symbol have such an odd English name, “ampersand”?

answer.es: Porque «ampersand» es una frase entera comprimida en una sola palabra.
answer.en: Because “ampersand” is a whole sentence squeezed into one word.

detail.es: El símbolo viene de una ligadura romana de las letras E y T, «et», documentada ya en grafitis de Pompeya. Cuando los niños recitaban el alfabeto y llegaban al final, añadían «and per se and» («y por sí sola, and»); con el tiempo ese trabalenguas se fundió en «ampersand».
detail.en: The symbol comes from a Roman ligature of the letters E and T, “et,” already documented in graffiti at Pompeii. When children recited the alphabet and reached the end, they added “and per se and” (“and, by itself, means ‘and’”); over time that tongue-twister fused into “ampersand.”

_evidence: contraction of and per se and, meaning "(the character) '&' by itself is 'and'"

question.es: ¿Qué tiene que ver el símbolo «#» con el peso de una libra?
question.en: What does the “#” symbol have to do with a unit of weight?

answer.es: Nació como la abreviatura latina de «libra», escrita tan rápido que se deformó.
answer.en: It started as the Latin abbreviation for “pound,” written so fast it warped.

detail.es: «Libra pondo» se abreviaba «lb», y los escribas trazaban una raya horizontal sobre las abreviaturas para dejar claro que iban unidas. Copiada deprisa una y otra vez, esa «lb» con barra terminó pareciéndose al tablero de tres en raya que hoy llamamos almohadilla.
detail.en: “Libra pondo” was abbreviated “lb,” and scribes drew a horizontal bar over abbreviations to show the letters belonged together. Copied fast, over and over, that barred “lb” ended up looking like the tic-tac-toe grid we call a hashtag today.

source: Mental Floss — Where Does the Hashtag Come From?
_evidence: people began abbreviating the Latin term for 'pound weight,' libra pondo, as lb. At the time, it was common to add a horizontal bar to abbreviations, known as a tittle, to show that the two letters were connected

question.es: ¿Para qué servía el signo de interrogación antes de escribir preguntas?
question.en: What was the question mark originally used for before marking questions?

answer.es: Para avisar a quien leía en voz alta de que debía subir el tono, como al cantar.
answer.en: To warn someone reading aloud that they should raise their pitch, like in a chant.

detail.es: En el siglo VIII, en el taller de manuscritos de Carlomagno, un escriba llamado Godescalc dibujó una especie de garabato ascendente sobre un punto para marcar dónde debía elevarse la voz al final de una frase. Solo hacia el siglo XIII se fijó como el símbolo exclusivo de la pregunta.
detail.en: In the 8th century, at Charlemagne’s manuscript workshop, a scribe named Godescalc drew a rising squiggle over a dot to mark where the voice should lift at the end of a sentence. Only by the 1200s did it settle into being the dedicated symbol for a question.

source: The Grammarphobia Blog — Who invented the question mark?
_evidence: The punctus interrogativus, a squiggle rising diagonally from left to right above a point, appeared in the late eighth century in Carolingian miniscule ... to tell reciters and singers when to raise their voices inquiringly and pause at the end of a question.

question.es: ¿Qué palabra latina se esconde apilada dentro del signo de exclamación?
question.en: What Latin word is stacked inside the exclamation mark?

answer.es: «Io», la interjección latina de alegría o triunfo.
answer.en: “Io,” the Latin interjection for joy or triumph.

detail.es: Los escribas italianos de alrededor del año 1400 escribían la «i» encima de la «o» al final de una frase de júbilo. Con el uso, ese apilamiento de dos letras se fue estilizando hasta quedar en el trazo vertical con un punto que usamos hoy.
detail.en: Italian scribes around the year 1400 wrote the “i” above the “o” at the end of a joyful sentence. With use, that stack of two letters got stylized down to the vertical stroke with a dot we use today.

source: Smithsonian Magazine — The History of the Exclamation Point
_evidence: In Latin, the exclamation of joy was io, where the i was written above the o.

question.es: ¿Por qué «island» en inglés lleva una «s» que no se pronuncia?
question.en: Why does English “island” carry an “s” that’s never pronounced?

answer.es: Porque hace 500 años alguien creyó, equivocado, que venía del latín «insula».
answer.en: Because 500 years ago someone wrongly assumed it came from Latin “insula.”

detail.es: La palabra inglesa antigua, «iland», no tiene relación de raíz con «isle», que sí viene del latín «insula» a través del francés. Aun así, hacia el siglo XVI los escribas emparentaron las dos palabras por su parecido y le injertaron la «s» a «island» para siempre.
detail.en: The Old English word, “iland,” has no root connection to “isle,” which really does come from Latin “insula” via French. Even so, by the 1500s scribes linked the two words by their resemblance and grafted the “s” onto “island” for good.

_evidence: The spelling of the first syllable was modified from 16c. by association with similar but unrelated isle.

question.es: ¿Por qué «debt» en inglés lleva una «b» que nadie pronuncia?
question.en: Why does English “debt” carry a “b” that nobody pronounces?

answer.es: Porque unos eruditos medievales se la injertaron a mano para que se pareciera al latín.
answer.en: Because medieval scholars grafted it in by hand to make it look more Latin.

detail.es: La palabra venía del francés «dete», sin be alguna. Al saber que el origen último era el latín «debitum», los escribas decidieron devolverle una letra que en la lengua hablada jamás había estado, ni en inglés ni en francés.
detail.en: The word came from French “dete,” with no b at all. Knowing the ultimate root was Latin “debitum,” scribes decided to give it back a letter that had never actually been spoken, in either English or French.

source: Merriam-Webster — Why Is ‘Debt’ Spelled Like That?
_evidence: They knew that the word had its origin in the Latin word debitum, and they thought it should pay homage to that word—and they had the wherewithal to slip a "b" into both the English and French versions of the word.

question.es: ¿Por qué «colonel» se escribe con «l» pero se pronuncia como si tuviera «r»?
question.en: Why is “colonel” spelled with an “l” but pronounced as if it had an “r”?

answer.es: Porque la ortografía copió al italiano y la pronunciación se quedó con el francés.
answer.en: Because the spelling copied Italian while the pronunciation stuck with French.

detail.es: El inglés tomó primero del francés «coronel», con erre. Hacia 1580 los eruditos volvieron a escribirlo como el italiano original, «colonnello», con ele, para parecer más cultos, pero la gente siguió diciéndolo como siempre. Las dos formas convivieron hasta 1650, y ganó la pronunciación antigua.
detail.en: English first borrowed French “coronel,” with an r. By the 1580s scholars started spelling it like the original Italian, “colonnello,” with an l, to look more learned, but people kept saying it the old way. Both forms coexisted until 1650, and the old pronunciation won out.

_evidence: The English spelling was modified in 1580s in learned writing to conform to the Italian form (via translations of Italian military manuals), and pronunciations with 'r' and 'l' coexisted until c. 1650, but the earlier pronunciation prevailed.

question.es: ¿De verdad existió una ley que permitía pegar a la mujer con un palo del grosor de un pulgar?
question.en: Was there really a law allowing a husband to beat his wife with a stick no wider than his thumb?

answer.es: No: esa «ley del pulgar» nunca existió. La frase viene de medir a ojo con el dedo.
answer.en: No — that “thumb law” never existed. The phrase comes from eyeballing measurements with your thumb.

detail.es: «Regla del pulgar» nació en el siglo XVII para describir un cálculo aproximado, usando la primera falange como unidad. El mito legal se atribuyó en 1976 a un juez del siglo XVIII sin que exista ningún registro de que lo dijera, y de ahí saltó a informes oficiales que lo repitieron como si fuera historia.
detail.en: “Rule of thumb” started in the 1600s to describe a rough calculation, using the first joint of the thumb as a unit. The legal myth was pinned in 1976 on an 18th-century judge with no record he ever said any such thing, and from there it leaked into official reports that repeated it as fact.

source: World Wide Words — Rule of thumb
_evidence: It is much more likely that it comes from the ancient use of bits of the body to make measurements ... The connection between 'rule of thumb' and wife-beating is actually a modern folk etymology, originating only in 1976

question.es: ¿«Salvado por la campana» viene de ataúdes con timbre para no enterrar vivos?
question.en: Does “saved by the bell” come from coffins fitted with bells to avoid burying people alive?

answer.es: No: es una expresión de boxeo. La campana que salva es la que acaba el asalto.
answer.en: No — it’s a boxing term. The bell that saves you is the one ending the round.

detail.es: Aparece documentada en la prensa deportiva de 1891, para el boxeador a punto de perder que se libra porque suena la campana del asalto. La leyenda de los ataúdes con cordón y campanilla es más vieja emocionalmente pero más joven en imprenta: no aparece hasta los años veinte del siglo XX.
detail.en: It shows up in sports pages from 1891, for the boxer about to lose who gets off the hook because the round-ending bell rings. The coffin-bell legend feels older emotionally but is younger in print: it doesn’t appear until the 1920s.

_evidence: comes to us, as should be no surprise, from the world of boxing. It originally and quite literally referred to a boxer who was about to be beaten into submission only to have the bell ring... This myth is silly but pernicious and is repeated by many who should know better.

question.es: ¿«Sleep tight» pide que aprietes las cuerdas de la cama antes de dormir?
question.en: Does “sleep tight” tell you to tighten the ropes on your bed before sleeping?

answer.es: No: «tight» ahí significa «bien, profundamente», no «apretado».
answer.en: No — “tight” there means “well, soundly,” not “tautly.”

detail.es: Las camas de cuerdas ya casi no se usaban cuando la frase aparece por primera vez, en 1866. Es la persona la que duerme «a fondo», no el colchón el que queda tenso: un uso del adverbio «tight» hoy raro pero antes corriente.
detail.en: Rope beds were nearly obsolete by the time the phrase first shows up, in 1866. It’s the person sleeping “soundly,” not the mattress staying taut — a use of the adverb “tight” that’s rare today but was once common.

_evidence: The word tightly, although not often used in this way now, means 'soundly, properly, well'... This explanation is a plausible guess but doesn't stand up to scrutiny.

question.es: ¿Por qué en inglés a alguien muy excéntrico se le compara con un sombrerero?
question.en: Why does English compare an eccentric person to a hat maker?

answer.es: Porque los sombrereros de verdad se intoxicaban con mercurio y temblaban sin control.
answer.en: Because real hat makers were poisoned by mercury and shook uncontrollably.

detail.es: El fieltro de los sombreros de copa se trataba con una solución de mercurio para «acartonar» el pelo animal, y respirar esos vapores durante años causaba temblores, habla confusa y alucinaciones, apodados «temblor del sombrerero». Estados Unidos no prohibió el mercurio en la industria hasta 1941.
detail.en: Top-hat felt was treated with a mercury solution to mat the animal fur, and breathing those fumes for years caused tremors, slurred speech and hallucinations, nicknamed “hatter’s shakes.” The US didn’t ban mercury in the industry until 1941.

source: History.com — Where did the phrase “mad as a hatter” come from?
_evidence: prolonged exposure to mercury caused employees to develop a variety of physical and mental ailments, including tremors (dubbed "hatter's shakes"), speech problems, emotional instability and hallucinations.

question.es: ¿Inventó el almirante Nelson la expresión «hacer la vista gorda»?
question.en: Did Admiral Nelson invent the expression “to turn a blind eye”?

answer.es: No: la frase ya existía un siglo antes de que él se llevara el telescopio al ojo ciego.
answer.en: No — the phrase already existed a century before he raised the telescope to his blind eye.

detail.es: El diccionario Oxford registra la expresión desde 1698. Nelson, tuerto desde 1794, la hizo famosa en 1801 al decir que no veía la orden de retirada de su superior en la batalla de Copenhague, y la anécdota se quedó tan pegada a la frase que mucha gente cree que nació ahí.
detail.en: The Oxford dictionary records the phrase from 1698. Nelson, blind in one eye since 1794, made it famous in 1801 by claiming he couldn’t see his superior’s order to withdraw at the Battle of Copenhagen — the anecdote stuck to the phrase so hard that many think it started there.

_evidence: The Oxford English Dictionary records usage of the phrase in 1698... The phrase to turn a blind eye is often associated with Vice-Admiral of the Blue Sir Horatio Nelson at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801.

question.es: ¿Por qué «robarle el trueno a alguien» significa apropiarse de su mérito?
question.en: Why does “stealing someone’s thunder” mean taking credit for their idea?

answer.es: Por un dramaturgo al que literalmente le robaron su máquina de hacer truenos.
answer.en: Because of a playwright whose literal thunder-making machine got stolen.

detail.es: John Dennis inventó en 1709 un nuevo método para simular truenos en el teatro, para una obra suya que fracasó. Poco después, otra compañía usó su técnica para representar «Macbeth» sin él, y Dennis se quejó: «No dejan que se represente mi obra, pero me roban el trueno».
detail.en: John Dennis invented a new way to simulate thunder onstage in 1709, for a play of his own that flopped. Soon after, another company used his technique to stage “Macbeth” without him, and Dennis complained: “They will not let my play run, but steal my thunder.”

_evidence: John Dennis invented a new method for simulating thunder sound effects for his 1709 tragedy "Appius and Virginia"... a later 1747 account attributed... "They will not let my play run, but steal my Thunder."

question.es: ¿Es literal la costumbre de «enterrar el hacha de guerra» al hacer las paces?
question.en: Is “burying the hatchet” to make peace a literal custom?

answer.es: Sí, y viene de un ritual real de paz entre pueblos indígenas de Norteamérica.
answer.en: Yes — it comes from a real peacemaking ritual among Native American nations.

detail.es: Documentado ya en 1680, el ritual consistía en enterrar de verdad hachas de guerra y otras armas en el suelo como sello público de un acuerdo de paz. El inglés adoptó la frase de forma figurada hacia 1754, y la mantiene desde entonces.
detail.en: Documented as early as 1680, the ritual involved literally burying war hatchets and other weapons in the ground as a public seal on a peace agreement. English picked up the phrase figuratively by 1754, and has kept it ever since.

_evidence: bury the hatchet "lay aside instruments of war, forget injuries and make peace" (1754) is from a Native American custom to conclude a peace-making, is described from 1680

question.es: ¿Por qué en inglés «eleven» y «twelve» no siguen el patrón de «trece, catorce»?
question.en: Why don’t English “eleven” and “twelve” follow the pattern of “thirteen, fourteen”?

answer.es: Porque literalmente significan «uno que sobra» y «dos que sobran» sobre diez.
answer.en: Because they literally mean “one left over” and “two left over” past ten.

detail.es: Vienen del germánico antiguo «ainlif» y «twalif»: contar hasta diez con los dedos y decir cuánto «queda» de más. El mismo patrón aparece en lituano, así que no es una rareza exclusivamente germánica.
detail.en: They come from Old Germanic “ainlif” and “twalif”: counting to ten on your fingers and naming how much is “left over.” The same pattern shows up in Lithuanian, so it isn’t a purely Germanic quirk.

_evidence: literally "one left" (over ten), from Proto-Germanic *ainlif-

question.es: ¿Por qué Lincoln empezó un discurso famoso diciendo «four score and seven years ago»?
question.en: Why did Lincoln open a famous speech with “four score and seven years ago”?

answer.es: Porque un «score» eran veinte años, la unidad con la que se contaban rebaños a muescas.
answer.en: Because a “score” meant twenty years — the unit used to count flocks by notches.

detail.es: Antes de tener papel a mano, los pastores tallaban una muesca por cada veinte cabezas de ganado que pasaban. Ese «veinte» de trabajo, «score», saltó del ganado al calendario, y ochenta y siete años se dicen «cuatro veintenas y siete».
detail.en: Before paper was handy, shepherds cut a notch for every twenty head of livestock that passed. That working “twenty,” the “score,” jumped from cattle to the calendar, and eighty-seven years became “four score and seven.”

_evidence: The notion probably is of counting large numbers (of a passing flock of sheep, etc.) by making a notch in a stick for each 20.

question.es: ¿Un billón tiene siempre el mismo número de ceros en todo el mundo de habla inglesa?
question.en: Does a “billion” always have the same number of zeros across the English-speaking world?

answer.es: No: hasta 1974 en el Reino Unido un billón valía mil veces más que en EE. UU.
answer.en: No — until 1974, a British “billion” was a thousand times bigger than an American one.

detail.es: El Reino Unido usaba la escala larga, donde un billón era un millón de millones, como sigue haciendo hoy el español. En 1974 el gobierno británico adoptó oficialmente la escala corta estadounidense, donde un billón es solo mil millones, para evitar confusiones internacionales.
detail.en: The UK used the long scale, where a billion meant a million million — the same system Spanish still uses today. In 1974 the British government officially adopted the American short scale, where a billion is just a thousand million, to avoid international confusion.

_evidence: After several decades of increasing informal British usage of the short scale, in 1974 the government of the UK adopted it, and it is used for all official purposes.

question.es: ¿Por qué una milla mide justo lo que mide?
question.en: Why does a mile measure exactly what it measures?

answer.es: Porque nació como mil pasos dobles de un soldado romano marchando.
answer.en: Because it started out as a thousand double-paces of a marching Roman soldier.

detail.es: «Mille» es «mil» en latín, y los romanos marcaban cada mil «passus» (cada paso completo, izquierda y derecha) con un mojón en sus calzadas. La palabra sobrevivió, pero la distancia exacta no: la milla inglesa medieval ya no coincidía con la romana original.
detail.en: “Mille” is Latin for “thousand,” and Romans marked every thousand “passus” (one full left-right stride) with a milestone along their roads. The word survived, but the exact distance didn’t: the medieval English mile no longer matched the original Roman one.

_evidence: from Latin milia "thousands," plural of mille "a thousand" ... An ancient Roman mile was 1,000 double paces

question.es: ¿Pudo una sola palabra ambigua precipitar el uso de la bomba atómica?
question.en: Could a single ambiguous word have helped trigger the use of the atomic bomb?

answer.es: Es la teoría más citada: el primer ministro japonés usó un término con dos lecturas.
answer.en: It’s the most-cited theory: Japan’s prime minister used a term with two readings.

detail.es: Al responder al ultimátum de Potsdam en 1945, Suzuki dijo que su gobierno iba a «mokusatsu» la propuesta: puede significar «sin comentarios por ahora» o «tratar con desprecio silencioso». Las agencias aliadas lo tradujeron como rechazo total, y Truman autorizó los bombardeos poco después.
detail.en: Responding to the Potsdam ultimatum in 1945, Suzuki said his government would “mokusatsu” the proposal — it can mean “no comment for now” or “treat with silent contempt.” Allied wire services translated it as outright rejection, and Truman authorized the bombings shortly after.

source: Universal Translation Services — The Mokusatsu Mistranslation
_evidence: To the Allied forces, it told that Prime Minister Suzuki and his government had outright rejected the Potsdam Declaration... Some think that Kantaro Suzuki knew that mokusatsu is an ambiguous word and decided to use it anyway.

question.es: ¿Por qué las estatuas antiguas de Moisés, incluida la de Miguel Ángel, le ponen cuernos?
question.en: Why do old statues of Moses, including Michelangelo’s, give him horns?

answer.es: Por una palabra hebrea que san Jerónimo tradujo mal al latín siglos antes.
answer.en: Because of a Hebrew word that Saint Jerome mistranslated into Latin centuries earlier.

detail.es: El hebreo «qaran» describe el rostro de Moisés brillando de luz tras hablar con Dios, pero comparte raíz con «qeren», cuerno. Jerónimo lo tradujo como «cornuta» en la Vulgata, y el error se convirtió en tradición artística hasta el siglo XVI.
detail.en: The Hebrew “qaran” describes Moses’s face shining with light after speaking with God, but it shares a root with “qeren,” horn. Jerome translated it as “cornuta” in the Vulgate, and the error became an artistic tradition well into the 1500s.

_evidence: Jerome translated the Hebrew term קָרַן (qāran, based on the root קֶרֶן qeren) as the Latin "cornuta" ("horned")... the term is now interpreted to mean 'shining' or 'emitting rays'

question.es: ¿Amenazó Jrushchov con enterrar a Occidente en un discurso de la Guerra Fría?
question.en: Did Khrushchev threaten to bury the West in a Cold War speech?

answer.es: Dijo eso literalmente, pero quería decir «os sobreviviremos», no una amenaza militar.
answer.en: He said exactly that, but meant “we will outlive you,” not a military threat.

detail.es: La frase «my vas pokhoronim» resume una idea marxista: el capitalismo cavaría su propia tumba y el socialismo seguiría en pie después. Al traducirse sin ese contexto ideológico en 1956, sonó a amenaza nuclear directa y disparó la alarma en la prensa occidental.
detail.en: The phrase “my vas pokhoronim” condenses a Marxist idea: capitalism would dig its own grave and socialism would still be standing afterward. Translated without that ideological context in 1956, it sounded like a direct nuclear threat and set off alarm in the Western press.

source: Russia Beyond — 'We will bury you': What Khrushchev actually meant
_evidence: Khrushchev was paraphrasing Karl Marx, who used to say that the proletariat is the undertaker of capitalism... What I had in mind was the outlook for the development of human society. Socialism will inevitably succeed capitalism.

question.es: ¿Se llamó Kennedy a sí mismo «un donut de mermelada» sin querer, ante todo Berlín?
question.en: Did Kennedy accidentally call himself “a jelly donut” in front of all Berlin?

answer.es: No: esa anécdota tan repetida no aparece en ningún sitio hasta 25 años después.
answer.en: No — that widely repeated anecdote doesn’t show up anywhere until 25 years later.

detail.es: «Ich bin ein Berliner» es la única forma gramaticalmente correcta de decir «soy berlinés» en ese contexto; el artículo «ein» era obligatorio. El chiste del donut lo publicó The New York Times en 1988, y desde entonces se repite como si el público de 1963 se hubiera reído en el momento, cosa que ninguna crónica de la época recoge.
detail.en: “Ich bin ein Berliner” is the only grammatically correct way to say “I am a Berliner” in that context; the article “ein” was required. The donut joke was published by The New York Times in 1988, and has been repeated ever since as if the 1963 crowd had laughed on the spot — something no contemporary account records.

source: Smithsonian Magazine — Where the Myth of JFK's 'Jelly Donut' Mistake Came From
_evidence: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' is not only correct but the one and only correct way of expressing in German what the President intended to say... Nobody laughed when he said this, as The New York Times would erroneously report twenty-five years later.
